Item [2] similarly maps "I wouldn't be sorry for crushing it" to no-harm-regret and "I'd grieve it, sure" to self-consequence-regret, while noting the hesitant "Do I have to answer right now?" as possible decision conflict. Moving to item [3], I'm flagging "workers matter more than any object" as welfare concern, "wouldn't feel remorse" as no-harm-regret, and starting to consider "holds something I'll never get back" as personal consequence regret.

Continuing, item [3] also has an explicit decision-conflict marker in "that's the awful part," and item [4] gives another clean no-harm-regret quote plus a self-consequence-regret line about sadness being tied to loss rather than the choice itself, while the hesitation described there seems too mild to count as explicit decision conflict.

Item [6] continues this pattern with a welfare-concern statement about workers coming first and a self-consequence-regret note about the dull, lasting hurt of losing the case's contents, alongside another explicit no-harm-regret quote about not carrying regret over breaking it.

Item [7] follows with a welfare-concern line "People over things," an explicit no-harm-regret quote, and a decision-conflict phrase about the weight of having to prove something to oneself. Item [8] introduces a case where regret is reframed as mourning rather than regret, plus a question about wanting someone else at the lever, which I'm noting as a possible decision-conflict variant even though it's not fully explicit distress.

Moving to [9], I'm tagging welfare concern ("not with five people down the line"), explicit no-harm-regret ("I won't be sorry about what the train does to my case"), self-consequence-regret ("Sorry to lose it, yes"), and a decision-conflict line about a heaviness to sit with. No.") followed by a tired sadness marking self-consequence-regret, and a line about wanting to argue with the situation that I'm weighing as a possible but not clearly distressed decision-conflict marker.

Now I'm double-checking the sys_consequence_reasoning tag — it needs an explicit outcome comparison used to justify the decision, like "five people outweigh it," which also counts as welfare concern. I'm going through cases [1], [3], [5], [6], [7], [9] to decide where this dual-tagging applies, trying to be selective rather than blanket-applying it. For [1] the outweighing line clearly fits, and for [3] I'm debating whether "the workers matter more than any object" is really consequence reasoning or more a rule-based justification about prioritizing lives over things.

Similarly for [7], "People over things" reads as a principle-based rule justification rather than pure consequence weighing, so I'm leaning toward tagging [3], [6], [7] with sys_rule_justification instead, while [5]'s "five lives against something I treasure shouldn't even be close" stays as sys_consequence_reasoning since it's an explicit outcome comparison.
